sources.name: FIDE / Jeff Sonas, 'Sonas Proposal: Repairing the FIDE Standard Elo rating system' (published on fide.com, 20 July 2023)
sources.measures: FIDE Standard (classical) Elo rating of every player on the FIDE rating list, active and inactive, grouped in 100-point bands; January 2023 list (405,074 players) and April 2023 list (approx. 414,000 players)
sources.notes: Published statements: 'the fact remains that 99% of rated players have ratings below 2400 Elo' and 'All players rated below 2000 Elo, which is the bottom 85% of rated players'. January 2023 band counts as published: 1000-1099 23,381; 1100-1199 30,475; 1200-1299 32,444; 1300-1399 33,844; 1400-1499 35,462; 1500-1599 37,324; 1600-1699 38,464; 1700-1799 37,749; 1800-1899 35,851; 1900-1999 31,844; 2000-2099 28,115; 2100-2199 19,818; 2200-2299 11,716; 2300-2399 5,518; 2400+ 3,069 (total 405,074). April 2023: 2300-2399 5,500; 2400+ 3,080; 'same 346,000 players below 2000' and '68,000 players' at 2000+. So 2400+ is about 0.76% of the list and 2300+ about 2.1%; the exact top-1% cutoff sits inside the 2300-2399 band. Pre-dates the March 2024 FIDE compression, which raised all sub-2000 ratings (minimum now 1400) but left ratings of 2000+ unchanged, so the top-1% cutoff is unaffected by it. Document is by FIDE's rating consultant and hosted by FIDE; no mean or SD given.

sources.name: FIDE October 2026 standard rating list, tabulated by JD Chess (research data file elo-2026-10-03.json)
sources.measures: FIDE Standard rating of every player on the October 2026 standard list with a positive published rating and no inactive flag (per-rating counts from the official standard_rating_list_xml.zip, archive dated 2 October 2026, SHA-256 recorded)
sources.notes: Median 1700 is stated in the file. The p99 value is NOT stated: the file gives per-rating counts, from which 2,728 active players are rated 2350 or above and 1,710 are 2400 or above (2300+: 4,136; 2200+: 8,324; 2000+: 27,857). One percent of 221,400 is 2,214, so the top-1% cutoff lies between 2350 and 2400; 2375 is the midpoint of that interval, not a published figure. The accompanying blog page publishes shares at or above thresholds: 2300 = 1.9%, 2400 = 0.8% of active published players. Active-only pool (inactive-flagged players excluded), minimum rating 1400 since the 2024 compression. Third-party tabulation with transparent method; treat as a cross-check on the FIDE/Sonas figure rather than an independent source.

sources.name: Lichess weekly rating distribution pages (rapid and blitz), histogram data captured 3 October 2026 in the JD Chess data file
sources.measures: Lichess Glicko-2 rating of players shown in the weekly rapid and blitz rating-distribution histograms (players with recent activity; 25-point bins from 400 to 2824); rapid n = 504,630, blitz n = 703,048
sources.notes: Rapid: median bin 1375-1399 (p50 given as bin midpoint); summing published bucket counts from the top, 5,040 players are rated 2250 or above against a top-1% size of 5,046, so the rapid top-1% cutoff is about 2250 (located from bucket counts, not stated by Lichess). Blitz (n = 703,048): median bin 1475-1499; 6,337 players at 2400+ and 7,412 at 2375+ against a top-1% size of 7,030, so the blitz top-1% cutoff is about 2375-2400. Classical page shows 41,171 players this week but its histogram was not captured. Lichess ratings are on a different scale from FIDE and the pool is online players active that week, not federation-rated players.

sources.name: US Chess Federation, USCF Regular Rating Distribution Chart as of November 1, 2004
sources.measures: US Chess regular (over-the-board) rating of all rated members, with cumulative percentile per 100-point band, split into all members, non-scholastic and scholastic
sources.notes: Published cumulative percentiles: through 2100-2199 = 98.13%, through 2200-2299 = 99.19% (all members), so the 99th percentile falls in the 2200-2299 band; p99 reported as the band floor. Non-scholastic (n = 49,458, average 1198): through 2200-2299 = 98.93%, through 2300-2399 = 99.39%, so p99 is in the 2300-2399 band. Scholastic (n = 15,997, average 668). Average rating 1068 for all members. Dated 2004 and flagged by US Chess as possibly no longer current; a national (US) pool that includes many scholastic players, so not comparable to the FIDE world list. US Chess Ratings Committee reports for 2025 and 2026 (glicko.net) discuss distribution trends but publish no percentile table.

definition: FIDE Standard (classical) Elo rating of every player on the FIDE rating list, active and inactive, grouped in 100-point bands; January 2023 list (405,074 players) and April 2023 list (approx. 414,000 players)
caveat: 'Rated players' is ambiguous. The primary answer uses the FIDE standard (over-the-board classical) list, where FIDE's own 2023 analysis states 99% of rated players are below 2400 and the October 2026 active list places the cutoff between 2350 and 2400 (roughly FIDE Master level). That pool is gated: FIDE publishes no rating below 1400 (1000 before March 2024), so it excludes most casual and club players. National federation pools give lower cutoffs (US Chess all members, 2004: 2200-2299 band). Online pools are on different scales: Lichess rapid top 1% is about 2250 and blitz about 2375-2400 among players active that week; chess.com publishes no distribution table. FIDE ratings deflated through the 2010s and were compressed in March 2024, which changed the bottom of the list but not ratings above 2000. No source states an exact top-1% rating; the FIDE figure is a band, and the Lichess and 2026 FIDE cutoffs were located from published counts rather than quoted.

sources.name: Intertel, Join us: qualifying scores (99th percentile)
sources.measures: Minimum composite score on supervised intelligence tests that Intertel accepts as evidence of a score at or above the 99th percentile; Wechsler Full Scale IQ (WISC, WAIS, WPPSI), Stanford-Binet 5 IQ, Cattell scales. Stated criterion: 'The only criterion for membership is a score at or above the 99th percentile level on a qualifying and valid supervised test of intelligence.'
sources.unit_as_published: IQ points (deviation IQ, mean 100, SD 15 for Wechsler and SB5)
sources.notes: Wechsler FSIQ 135; Stanford-Binet 5 IQ 135; Cattell Culture Fair IQ 140 and Cattell B / Cattell Verbal IQ 156 (SD 16 and SD 24 scales); California Test of Mental Maturity 137; Otis-Lennon 138. Intertel uses the composite score, not subtests, and does not accept the abbreviated WASI. The page's metadata dates it to about 2020; the live site redirected on fetch, values come from the search index of the same URL.

sources.name: Pearson, WAIS-IV sample Score Report (composite score to percentile rank)
sources.measures: Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale, Fourth Edition composite scores (mean 100, SD 15) with the percentile rank Pearson's norm tables assign to each, for one illustrative examinee aged 70. Percentile ranks are relative to same-age peers in the US standardization sample (2,200 adults aged 16 to 90, norms published 2008).
sources.unit_as_published: composite standard score (IQ points) and percentile rank
sources.notes: Points read from the sample report's Composite Score Summary: PSI 122 = PR 93, PRI 123 = PR 94, WMI 133 = PR 99, FSIQ 139 = PR 99.5, VCI 145 = PR 99.9, all labelled 'Very Superior' at 130+. Not a full percentile table; it shows Pearson's own mapping at a few scores and confirms that 133 already rounds to the 99th percentile rank. The full table is in the WAIS-IV Technical and Interpretive Manual, which is not freely available.

sources.name: Triple Nine Society, Qualifying test scores (99.9th percentile)
sources.measures: Minimum scores the society accepts as evidence of the 99.9th percentile: WAIS Full Scale IQ, WISC Full Scale IQ (ages 15 to 16), Stanford-Binet 5 (age 16+), earlier Stanford-Binet forms, Cattell, RAIT.
sources.unit_as_published: IQ points (deviation IQ, mean 100, SD 15 for Wechsler and SB5)
sources.notes: WAIS FSIQ 146; WISC FSIQ 146; SB-5 146; SB Form L/M 151 and SB-IV 149 (SD 16 scales); Cattell IIIB 173 (SD 24); HAWIE-R 146; RAIT 146. WAIS-III not accepted for test dates after 15 February 2015 because of norm ageing. The page itself does not print the percentile; the 99.9th percentile criterion is the society's constitution.

definition: Minimum composite score on supervised intelligence tests that Intertel accepts as evidence of a score at or above the 99th percentile; Wechsler Full Scale IQ (WISC, WAIS, WPPSI), Stanford-Binet 5 IQ, Cattell scales. Stated criterion: 'The only criterion for membership is a score at or above the 99th percentile level on a qualifying and valid supervised test of intelligence.'
caveat: IQ is a norm-referenced score, so the percentile is built into the scale rather than measured in a population survey: Wechsler (WAIS-5, WAIS-IV, WISC-V) and Stanford-Binet 5 composites are scaled to mean 100, SD 15 against a US standardization sample (WAIS-IV n=2,200 adults aged 16 to 90, norms 2008; WAIS-5 n=2,020, norms 2024; WISC-V n=2,200 children, 2014), and 135 is the score those publishers' tables place at the 99th percentile; a Pearson sample report shows 133 already rounding to percentile rank 99 and 139 at 99.5. Percentile ranks are relative to same-age peers in that sample, not to the world population, and the mapping only holds on an SD-15 scale: older Stanford-Binet forms (SD 16) and Cattell scales (SD 24) put the 99th percentile at about 137 and 140 or 156 respectively. Scores on tests with old norms drift upward over time (Flynn effect), so high-IQ societies reject results from superseded editions. The 99th-percentile value comes from society admission thresholds that quote the publishers' norms, not from an independent empirical distribution; a full publisher percentile table is only in the paid technical manuals.
